item.title: Dirac Propagation for Simulating Fermionic Observables under Particle-Number-Conserving Unitaries
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Discarding Dirac operator strings with weight w>min⁡(N,M−N) yields exact expectation values under particle-number-conserving unitaries, bounding retained terms to TN=∑q=0min⁡(N,M−N)(Mq)2∈𝒪~(M2min⁡(N,M−N)).

Grade 0.420 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · G Arnav Naidu, Matteo D'Anna, Adrián Pérez-Salinas, Jannes Nys, Juan Carrasquilla

Figure

Number of doublons versus time t following a quench of D=2 doublons on a 6×6 Fermi-Hubbard lattice across different interaction strengths U/t and truncation thresholds ε compared to exact diagonalization.

Asks

Can Heisenberg-picture observable propagation for particle-number-conserving fermionic unitaries avoid exponential operator growth at fixed particle number?

Before

General Pauli and Majorana propagation scale exponentially with system size even at low particle filling.

But

Scaling becomes exponential when particle number N is a constant non-zero filling fraction of modes M. Dynamics must strictly conserve particle number.

Tools

Dirac operator canonical and hole bases · Dirac-weight truncation cutoff · Adjoint Lie-algebraic splitting rules

Abstract

Simulating the dynamics of interacting fermions remains a central computational challenge across physics and chemistry. We introduce Dirac propagation, a classical method that simulates local observables in fermionic systems subject to particle-number-conserving unitaries. We show that, in the operator expansion, strings with weights above the total particle number can be discarded without incurring any error in the final expectation value. This exact cutoff bounds the number of retained strings polynomially in the number of modes at fixed particle number, including for interacting dynamics. The formalism combines a compact representation with explicit expressions for interacting gates and exact treatment of number-conserving fermionic Gaussian and Clifford unitaries. This framework offers an approach to simulating fermionic many-body dynamics and classically benchmarking fermionic quantum circuits.

item.title: Blueprint for DOE Quantum Supercomputing
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Defines DOE deployment roadmap targeting first-generation fault-tolerant quantum computers with ≥100 logical qubits executing 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations by 2028, scaling to production systems with 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits and 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations in the 2030s.

Grade 0.402 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Ryan Bennink, Robin Blume-Kohout, Salman Habib, Andrew Landahl, Hai Ah Nam, Laura Schulz, Mallikarjun Shankar, Nicholas Wright

Asks

What strategy, milestones, and technical requirements must the DOE adopt to integrate fault-tolerant quantum computers into US national scientific computing infrastructure?

But

Strategic roadmap based on commercial hardware projections and anticipated error-correction thresholds rather than empirical multi-system deployment.

Tools

Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) · Quantum error correction architectures · High-performance computing (HPC) integration frameworks · Quantum-centric supercomputing system software

Abstract

Quantum computing stands at the threshold of a transformative decade, where the field will evolve from small-scale demonstrations toward practical scientific computing at scale. This Blueprint identifies fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs) as a viable, scalable, and broadly applicable path to achieving "quantum scientific utility." It outlines a strategy to prepare the US Department of Energy (DOE) for FTQCs and their integration into the US national scientific computing infrastructure. Its purpose is to identify the steps, milestones, and research directions necessary for DOE to enable initial deployment of FTQCs in 2028 as a scientific tool for the nation and mature this capability into the 2030s. Given recent demonstrations of logical operations on error-corrected logical qubits and the advancement of commercial hardware roadmaps, DOE should begin preparations for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing deployment for DOE science missions. This Blueprint proposes that DOE focus on (1) deploying first-generation scientifically relevant quantum computers with at least 100 logical qubits and performing at least 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations in scientifically relevant calculations; (2) developing essential FTQC programming competencies, system software, and facility readiness; and (3) investing in cutting-edge focused R&D that fosters breakthroughs in scientific applications, algorithms, and logical architectures needed to accelerate the advent of scientific utility. This effort will position DOE to transition to larger systems: production-scale quantum computers that comprise 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits, perform 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations, and execute scientifically useful computations at scale. The Blueprint calls for transformative R&D and collective action to accelerate the advent of scientific quantum utility and bring it within reach by 2028.

item.title: Exploiting SU(2) Symmetry for Efficient Quantum State Preparation of Matrix Product States
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Exploiting non-Abelian spin SU(2) symmetry via the Wigner-Eckart theorem reduces the Toffoli cost of sequential matrix product state compilation by factors of 2.4–3.7 over U(1) compilation and 26–68 over dense compilation at b=21 angle bits.

Grade 0.384 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Etienne D'Argenlieu, Alessandro Summer, Franccois Jamet, David P. Tew, Lachlan P. Lindoy

Figure

Ratio of Toffoli counts for U(1) versus SU(2) compilation and dense versus SU(2) compilation as a function of bond dimension χ across Hubbard cylinders and Anderson impurity models.

Asks

How can non-Abelian spin SU(2) symmetry be exploited to reduce the fault-tolerant quantum circuit cost of matrix product state preparation?

Before

U(1)-adapted sequential compilation and standard dense compilation (Bauer 2024, Malz 2024), yielding Toffoli counts 2.4 to 68 times higher for the same states.

But

Requires exact spin-rotation invariance; systems with Zeeman fields or generic spin-orbit coupling break the symmetry. Target state must have a fixed, definite total spin chosen before compilation.

Tools

matrix product states · Wigner-Eckart theorem · Clements unitary synthesis · Clebsch-Gordan transformations · fault-tolerant Toffoli cost modeling

Abstract

Quantum computing offers a promising route to simulating strongly correlated systems, particularly for dynamical and spectral quantities whose classical computation can become prohibitively expensive. Fault-tolerant algorithms for these tasks, including real-time dynamics and phase estimation, assume efficient preparation of the initial many-body state, making state preparation an important bottleneck. Matrix product states obtained classically with the density matrix renormalization group can be compiled sequentially into fault-tolerant circuits. We exploit non-Abelian spin SU(2) symmetry in this compilation. By the Wigner-Eckart theorem, only the reduced tensors, which carry the variational information, need generic unitary synthesis. The magnetic structure is restored by Clebsch-Gordan transformations with analytically known angles. We benchmark the method on representative strongly correlated models, including the one-dimensional Hubbard model, quasi-one-dimensional Hubbard geometries, and Anderson impurity models, and perform fault-tolerant resource estimates using the Toffoli count as the primary cost metric. Across the systems considered, exploiting non-Abelian SU(2) symmetry reduces the Toffoli cost roughly threefold relative to U(1)-adapted compilation and by more than an order of magnitude relative to the standard dense compilation method. These results demonstrate how non-Abelian symmetries can substantially reduce the cost of transferring classically tractable many-body ground states to quantum computers, facilitating their use in quantum dynamics and energy estimation.

item.title: Thermal state preparation with shallow quantum circuits
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — PP-VarQITE produces state-preparation circuits that are two to ten times shallower than sequential MPS compilations across frustrated chains and 2D lattices, running on Quantinuum Helios-1 up to 98 qubits at two-qubit depth at most 42.

Grade 0.381 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Cenk Tüysüz, Simon Deconihout, Enrico Rinaldi, Michele Grossi

Figure

Absolute thermal energy-density error versus native two-qubit gate count (left) and depth (right) for a 50-site frustrated chain (top) and a 7×7 TFIM (bottom), showing PP-VarQITE outperforming MPS compilation routes in circuit depth.

Asks

How can finite-temperature thermal states be prepared within shallow circuit depths on noisy quantum hardware using purely classical parameter determination?

Before

Sequential matrix-product-state compilation, which incurs an order-of-magnitude larger gate count and circuit depth to match accuracy.

But

Suffers from an imaginary-time variational delay at intermediate temperatures in frustrated and 2D systems; classical parameter generation requires truncating retained Pauli terms above coefficient threshold cmin⁡.

Tools

Pauli propagation · variational quantum imaginary-time evolution (VarQITE) · thermal purification · Quantinuum Helios-1 trapped-ion processor · Bell-frame recompilation

Abstract

Preparing thermal states on noisy quantum hardware requires circuits that remain shallow at low temperatures. Even when accurate classical state representations are available, compiling them into suitable circuits can be costly. We introduce PP-VarQITE, combining Pauli propagation with variational quantum imaginary-time evolution to determine circuit parameters entirely classically, with target temperatures encoded in the angles of a fixed circuit architecture. In numerical studies of Ising and frustrated Heisenberg models, we recover low-temperature energies and correlations using up to 100 qubits. Across the frustrated chain and two-dimensional lattice, our circuits are approximately two to ten times shallower than the lowest-depth circuits from sequential tensor-network compilation. These shallow circuits enable us to prepare a 48-site frustrated chain and a 7×7 Ising lattice using 96 and 98 qubits on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. We reproduce the development of dimer order and lattice-wide correlations from high to low temperatures, with the lattice circuits requiring at most 42 two-qubit layers. Through classical circuit design, we demonstrate low-temperature state preparation at circuit sizes beyond the practical reach of statevector simulation.

item.title: Machine Learning-Based Quantum Error Mitigation for Bound-State Simulations
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Residual learning with exact Frobenius-norm convex projection onto valid density matrices estimates ground-state energy as -0.134 MeV (ideal -0.135 MeV, fidelity 0.999) for a 3-qubit Λ-deuteron model, and -3.014 MeV and -3.045 MeV (fidelities 0.995 and 0.998) for 4-qubit Λ-α potentials.

Grade 0.379 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Sumit Choudhary, Tarunpreet Kaur, Harjeet Kaur, Harpreet Singh

Figure

Ground-state energy in MeV (top) and quantum state fidelity (bottom) versus training-set size N for the 3-qubit system. Proposed ML-QEM (blue) converges stably to the exact energy and unity fidelity, whereas conventional ML-QEM (red) drops below the ground-state energy.

Asks

Can residual learning combined with convex projection to physical density matrices improve machine learning-based quantum error mitigation for hypernuclear ground-state simulations?

Before

Unmitigated hardware estimates deviated substantially, and conventional ML-QEM predicted unphysical energies below exact ground-state values (e.g. -3.822 MeV and -3.739 MeV for 4-qubit potentials).

But

Evaluated on 3-qubit and 4-qubit mapped Hamiltonians; required 1600 VQE-ansatz training states, whereas Haar-random training states failed to recover target ground states.

Tools

Residual ML regression (ridge and RBF kernel ridge) · Frobenius-norm convex projection onto density matrices · IBM Quantum hardware · Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE)

Code. https://zenodo.org/records/23969830

Abstract

Noise in quantum devices remains a major challenge for reliable quantum simulations, making quantum error mitigation an important tool for improving their accuracy. Machine learning-based quantum error mitigation (ML-QEM) provides a useful approach, but its performance depends on the training datasets and may produce reconstructed quantum states that are not physically valid. In this work, we introduce an ML-QEM framework that uses residual learning with convex projection to ensure that reconstructed density matrices satisfy physically valid density matrices. We study the effect of different training datasets and regression models using Haar-random and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) ansatz states. We compare the proposed approach with conventional ML-QEM, readout error mitigation, and zero-noise extrapolation. The method is tested on IBM quantum hardware for three- and four-qubit simulations of the bound Λ-deuteron and Λ-α hypernuclear systems, respectively. For the three-qubit system, ridge regression trained on VQE-ansatz states gives a ground-state energy of -0.134 MeV, close to the ideal value of -0.135 MeV, with a state fidelity of 0.999. For four-qubit system, kernel ridge regression gives ground-state energies of -3.014 and -3.045 MeV, with corresponding state fidelities of 0.995 and 0.998. These results show that physically constrained reconstruction, along with the choice of training datasets and regression models, can improve ML-QEM performance for the quantum simulations studied in this work.

item.title: Coherent meson-baryon conversion in a cold-atom non-Abelian lattice gauge simulator
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Realized non-Abelian lattice gauge dynamics with dynamical matter in a cold-atom quantum simulator, mapping an analog system to a gauge sector of a truncated 1D SU(2) quantum link model and observing coherent meson-to-baryon–antibaryon oscillations.

Grade 0.377 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum simulations with ultracold quantum gases” · Tian-Yi Wang, Wei-Yong Zhang, Tie-Jin Zhong, Ming-Gen He, Zhao-Yu Zhou, Hui Sun, Zhen-Sheng Yuan, Jian-Wei Pan

Figure

Coherent real-time dynamics between meson population and baryon–antibaryon pairs near the bare resonance g2=−16m/3, showing anti-correlated population oscillations versus evolution time.

Asks

Can non-Abelian gauge-matter interactions and hadronic dynamics with dynamical matter be engineered and microscopically resolved in an analog cold-atom simulator?

But

Truncated link representation (jmax⁡=1/2) restricted to the non-zero Gauss-charge sector 𝐆ˆℓ2=2, Gˆℓz=1 in a 1D chain of up to 20 sites.

Tools

ultracold ⁸⁷Rb atoms in two hyperfine states · spin-dependent optical superlattice · resonant tunneling via magnetic-field gradient · site- and spin-resolved quantum gas microscopy with transverse Stern–Gerlach separation

Abstract

Quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the non-Abelian gauge theory of quarks and gluons, provides a microscopic description of strongly interacting matter, including hadron structure and dynamics. Real-time dynamics and finite-density properties of these systems remain challenging for conventional Monte Carlo methods because of sign problems. Quantum simulation provides a complementary approach, although circuit depth and noise limit digital implementations and non-Abelian gauge-matter interactions remain difficult to engineer in analog systems. Here we realize a non-Abelian lattice gauge model with dynamical matter in an analog cold-atom simulator and directly observe its hadronic dynamics using site- and spin-resolved quantum gas microscopy. This realization is enabled by harnessing two hyperfine states and site-occupation configurations of 87Rb atoms to jointly encode both matter and gauge fields. We tailor resonant tunneling in a spin-dependent optical superlattice to implement a gauge sector of a truncated one-dimensional SU(2) quantum link model with independently tunable mass and gauge coupling. Leveraging this control, we track the conversion of an initially mesonic state into baryonic or vacuum-like configurations through slow mass ramps. Near resonance, we observe coherent oscillations between mesons and baryon-antibaryon pairs and characterize the conversion efficiency as a function of mass, gauge coupling and net baryon density. Our realization establishes an atomic platform for non-Abelian gauge dynamics, opening a route to microscopic studies of nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly interacting matter.

item.arxave:abstract: Quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the non-Abelian gauge theory of quarks and gluons, provides a microscopic description of strongly interacting matter, including hadron structure and dynamics. Real-time dynamics and finite-density properties of these systems remain challenging for conventional Monte Carlo methods because of sign problems. Quantum simulation provides a complementary approach, although circuit depth and noise limit digital implementations and non-Abelian gauge-matter interactions remain difficult to engineer in analog systems. Here we realize a non-Abelian lattice gauge model with dynamical matter in an analog cold-atom simulator and directly observe its hadronic dynamics using site- and spin-resolved quantum gas microscopy. This realization is enabled by harnessing two hyperfine states and site-occupation configurations of 87Rb atoms to jointly encode both matter and gauge fields. We tailor resonant tunneling in a spin-dependent optical superlattice to implement a gauge sector of a truncated one-dimensional SU(2) quantum link model with independently tunable mass and gauge coupling. Leveraging this control, we track the conversion of an initially mesonic state into baryonic or vacuum-like configurations through slow mass ramps. Near resonance, we observe coherent oscillations between mesons and baryon-antibaryon pairs and characterize the conversion efficiency as a function of mass, gauge coupling and net baryon density. Our realization establishes an atomic platform for non-Abelian gauge dynamics, opening a route to microscopic studies of nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly interacting matter.

item.title: Trotterized hybrid qubit-boson simulation of the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard model
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Trotterized Bosonic Qiskit simulation of a single polariton on an 8-site Jaynes–Cummings–Hubbard chain tracks exact diagonalization with site occupation errors bounded between 10−4 and 10−2, peaking at 6.98×10−3.

Grade 0.375 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Nabaraj Khatri, Dilip Ojha, Rajib Tripathi, Kismat K. C, Ashish Khanal

Figure

Absolute occupation discrepancy |⟨ni⟩Trotter−⟨ni⟩Exact| versus time across 8 individual sites for a single initial polariton, showing saturation within 10−4 to 10−2.

Asks

Can Bosonic Qiskit with a Matrix Product State backend accurately capture many-body real-time dynamics in a Jaynes–Cummings–Hubbard lattice when benchmarked against exact diagonalization?

But

One-dimensional open chains with Fock cutoff d=2 (hard-core photon limit), first-order Trotter decomposition with time step Δt=0.05, and restricted to low excitation numbers (1 or 2).

Tools

Bosonic Qiskit · Matrix Product State (MPS) backend · Trotterized circuit decomposition · Exact diagonalization benchmark

Abstract

The Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard (JCH) model describes the interaction of light and matter in coupled optical cavities and provides a framework for studying their quantum dynamics. In this work, we design a Trotterized quantum circuit to investigate the real-time dynamics of the JCH model using Bosonic Qiskit and a Matrix Product State (MPS) backend. We simulate single-polariton transport and benchmark site occupations against exact diagonalization results. We then extend the simulations to the two-excitation sector under a hard-core photon constraint, examining excitation transport and symmetry properties. Finally, we study the dependence of bipartite entanglement entropy on the inter-cavity photon-hopping strength. The results illustrate how hybrid qubit-boson circuits, simulated with matrix product states, can be used to study light-matter lattice dynamics. This work provides a numerical benchmark for extending hybrid simulation approaches to more complex interacting and open light-matter systems.

item.title: Classical algorithms for sparse random Hamiltonians via free probability
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Classical algorithm evaluates spectral fluctuations, partition functions, thermal values, and TOC/OTOC correlation functions to error ε in (1/ε)2+o(1) time for sparse random Pauli Hamiltonians.

Grade 0.354 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum simulations with ultracold quantum gases” · Matthew Ding, Robbie King, Thomas Schuster

Figure

Exact values versus classical algorithm predictions as free-cumulant truncation order ℓ increases from 2 to 12 for the spectral amplitude, partition function, TOC, and OTOC on an instance with m=80,n=18.

Asks

Can quantum computers yield generic, scalable advantages when simulating quantum many-body systems in traditionally complex, average-case regimes?

Before

Existing classical methods required exponential time due to sign problems and entanglement growth at late evolution times and low temperatures.

But

Applies to fully non-local sparse Pauli Hamiltonians, subexponential precision ε=1/2o(n/log⁡n), and evolution times and inverse temperatures scaling up to 𝒪(n/log⁡n).

Tools

free probability theory · free cumulants · diagrammatic resummation · commutation graph statistics · hypercontractivity

Abstract

The search for quantum advantage in average-case problems is a pressing open question in physics and computer science. The widest conjectured example of such an advantage is in simulation of quantum many-body systems, where sign problems and entanglement growth cause the breakdown of many classical methods. Nonetheless, theoretical evidence for or against such an advantage remains scarce. Here, we investigate this in sparse random non-local Hamiltonians. We design a classical algorithm for such Hamiltonians that enables accurate computation of spectral fluctuations, thermal values, and time-ordered and out-of-time-order correlation functions. For any subexponential precision ε, our algorithm runs in time (1/ε)^(2+o(1)), nearly identical to a quantum simulation. Crucially, this applies even at late evolution times, low temperatures, and near critical points, where existing classical methods require exponential time. Rather than directly simulating a quantum state or operator, our algorithm first computes the model's mean behavior and then a short hierarchy of instance-dependent corrections. These corrections predict long-time behavior based on short-time data using free probability theory.
